data.text/markdown:
Tutorial 4: Monitoring a cat qubit, quantum trajectories with dynamiqs

The three previous tutorials simulate the average evolution of a cat qubit with the Lindblad master equation. In this challenge the buffer output of the cat is measured, continuously, and we want to know what a single run looks like given its measurement record. This is the realm of quantum trajectories (unravelings of the master equation). dynamiqs ships four stochastic solvers; we use two of them:
  • dq.jssesolve: jump unraveling, the record is a list of click times (photon counting),
  • dq.dssesolve: diffusive unraveling, the record is a noisy continuous signal (homodyne or heterodyne detection).
Along the way we meet the central physical fact of the challenge: the buffer channel is dark as long as the memory sits in the code space, and shines when it does not. Everything is in units of ||(\kappa_2 = 1||) (see docs/THEORY.md). The helper package catchtheflip builds the models and wraps the solvers; feel free to look at its source, it is short.

1. The model and its channels

We use a small, deliberately noisy cat (||(\bar n = 1.5||), strong dephasing) so that bit flips happen within a few hundred time units. The challenge device is quieter and bigger.

console.name: stdout
console.text:
channels: ('buffer', 'loss', 'thermal', 'dephasing')
  buffer     jump operator of shape (16, 16)
  loss       jump operator of shape (16, 16)
  thermal    jump operator of shape (16, 16)
  dephasing  jump operator of shape (16, 16)

data.text/markdown: The buffer channel ||(L_2 = \sqrt{\kappa_2}(a^2 - \alpha^2)||) annihilates both ||(|\pm\alpha\rangle||): its click rate ||(\langle L_2^\dagger L_2\rangle||) vanishes in the code space. Kick the memory out (here: add one photon with ||(a^\dagger||)) and the channel lights up.

console.name: stdout
console.text:
buffer click rate in |+alpha>        : 0.000
buffer click rate in a^dag |+alpha>  : 2.400

data.text/markdown:
2. One trajectory: watch the cat flip

simulate.long_trajectory runs dq.jssesolve with all channels unravelled as jumps and records ||(\langle Z_L\rangle(t) = 1 - 2P(x<0)||), the expectation of the Z readout of the conditional state, together with the click times of every channel. Only the buffer clicks are observable in the challenge; the others are privileged information that we use here to understand what happens.

Two things to notice.
  1. Loss clicks do nothing visible: ||(a|\alpha\rangle = \alpha|\alpha\rangle||), the state is an eigenstate of the jump. (They flip the parity, i.e. the logical ||(X||), which we do not plot.)
  2. Thermal and dephasing clicks kick the state out of the code space; the buffer then sometimes clicks while the stabilisation brings the state back. Most of the time the state comes back to the same lobe. Occasionally ||(\langle Z_L\rangle||) drops: a bit flip. Look at where it drops to. What the conditional state is after a flip, and why, is a question of step 1 of the challenge.
Zoom on the buffer click that pulled ||(\langle Z_L\rangle||) down the most, and look at what happens before and after it. Do not expect a fireworks display with this small cat: the burst of a flip is of order ||(\bar n^2 \kappa_2 \tau||) photons, only a few at ||(\bar n = 1.5||), and many drops of ||(\langle Z_L\rangle||) in this unraveling are gradual (one dephasing kick at a time). The burst grows quickly with the cat size; that is the point of step 2 of the challenge. Statistically, though, flip segments do carry more buffer clicks (section 3).

console.name: stdout
console.text:
buffer click at t = 35.0: <Z_L> from 0.59 to 0.47
buffer clicks per unit time over the whole run: 0.08

data.text/markdown:
3. Segments, readout and labels

The challenge data are segments: the memory is prepared in ||(|+\alpha\rangle||), monitored for ||(T_{\rm seg}||), then read out in ||(Z||). simulate.counting_segments returns, for each segment, the buffer click times and pneg, the probability that the readout gives ||(-\alpha||) (the weight of the conditional state on ||(x<0||)). The label of a segment is a sample of that readout (records.sample_labels).

console.name: stdout
console.text:
flip probability per segment: 0.097  (29 flips in 300 segments)
mean buffer clicks: flip segments 2.79, others 1.59

data.text/markdown: The average over segments must agree with the master equation: this is the standard sanity check of any trajectory simulation (and of the time step dt).

console.name: stdout
console.text: P(-alpha at T_seg): trajectories 0.0909 +- 0.0076, master equation 0.0843

data.text/markdown: And the rates can be read off the Liouvillian spectrum without any time evolution: ||(\langle Z_L\rangle(t) = e^{-\Gamma_Z t}||) gives ||(P(-\alpha, T) = (1 - e^{-\Gamma_Z T})/2||).

console.name: stdout
console.text:
Gamma_Z = 8.643e-03  (T_Z = 116),  Gamma_X = 7.390e-02  (2 kappa_1 [(1 + 2 n_th) nbar + n_th] = 0.076)
predicted P(-alpha, 20) = 0.0794

data.text/markdown:
4. A first detector, and the challenge metrics

Count the buffer clicks of each segment and rank the segments by that count. The leaderboard discards the 30 % most suspicious segments, computes the residual flip fraction ||(\rho_{70}||) among the rest (catchtheflip.scoring.rho_at_yield) and reports the flip suppression ||(1 - \rho_{70}||) (higher is better); the AUC summarises the whole ranking. Try a smarter feature, for example the maximum number of clicks in any window of two time units: bursts are short. (The segments of this tutorial last 20 time units to keep it fast. The challenge datasets use segments of 200, at four cat sizes mixed in one file.)

console.name: stdout
console.text:
total clicks                  : AUC = 0.625, 1 - rho_70 = 0.21 (13 of 29 flips discarded with 30 % of the segments)
max clicks in a window of 2   : AUC = 0.633, 1 - rho_70 = 0.26 (14 of 29 flips discarded with 30 % of the segments)

data.text/markdown: With this small, noisy cat the bursts are weak (a flip emits about ||(\bar n^2 \kappa_2\tau||) photons) and the background of kicks is strong, so the ranking is poor. The challenge device has bigger cats, from ||(\bar n = 2||) to ||(3.5||). Part of your job is to understand how the burst, the background and the flip rate scale with ||(\bar n||), and what a good ranking is worth for a logical qubit (docs/THEORY.md, section 7, and step 4 of the challenge).

5. Heterodyne records

Real buffer outputs are usually measured with a heterodyne detector rather than a photon counter. simulate.heterodyne_segments returns the two quadratures ||(I||) and ||(Q||) of the output field, binned in time, with white noise of variance (1/bin duration) on top, for a detection efficiency eta. The expected signal during a burst is ||(\sqrt{2\eta}\,\mathrm{Re}\langle a^2 - \alpha^2\rangle \approx -\sqrt{2\eta}\,\alpha^2||): negative, in the ||(I||) quadrature. A word on the integrator. heterodyne_segments uses the scheme of Rouchon and Ralph (dq.method.Rouchon1), which keeps the state physical at every step. The textbook Euler-Maruyama scheme (method="euler") is fine for this short segment of a small cat. For the segments of the challenge (200 time units, cats up to ||(\bar n = 3.5||)) it is not: rare large noise increments scramble the state, and the flip probability comes out two to four times too large, whatever the time step. A stochastic simulation that runs is not yet a simulation that is right: compare its average with the master equation, as in section 3.

console.name: stdout
console.text: I record standard deviation: 2.22  (white noise: sqrt(1/0.2) = 2.24 )

data.text/markdown:
6. The buffer as a real mode

In the device the buffer is a resonator with decay rate ||(\kappa_b||), not an abstract channel. models.two_mode builds the memory + buffer model; its monitored channel is ||(i\sqrt{\kappa_b}\, b \simeq \sqrt{\kappa_2}(a^2 - \alpha^2)||) (the phase ||(i||) gives the burst the same sign as in the single-mode model). The adiabatic elimination of section 2 of the primer predicts the same physics with ||(\kappa_2 = 4 g_2^2 / \kappa_b||), and a buffer that lights up during a flip. The fixed-step integrator needs a smaller step here (dt=1e-3): the Hamiltonian terms of the two-mode model make larger steps unstable. (method="event" selects the adaptive event-based integrator of dynamiqs instead, whose maximum step dtmax sets how precisely the click times are resolved. Whatever the integrator, validate it against the master equation before trusting it.)

Exercises

  1. Increase nbar to 2 and 2.5 (and N accordingly). How do the burst size and the number of background clicks per segment change? How does the flip probability change?
  2. Leave the dephasing channel unmonitored: simulate the segments with the stochastic master equation dq.jsmesolve(m.H, m.jump_ops, thetas=[0, 0, 0, 0], etas=[1, 1, 1, 0], ...) (efficiency 0 for the dephasing channel, whose effect is then averaged in the master equation; use method=dq.method.EulerJump(dt=...) and a tsave tuple whose times are multiples of dt). Does the record of the buffer channel change its statistics? Does the conditional ||(\langle Z_L\rangle(t)||) look the same?
  3. Compute ||(\Gamma_Z||) from the spectrum for ||(\bar n = 1, 1.5, \dots, 4||) and plot ||(\log \Gamma_Z||) against ||(\bar n||). Which error channel sets the slope?
Each exercise defines new variables: in marimo a global name can be defined in one cell only, so pick new names (p_ex1, m_ex1, seg_ex1, …) or cell-local ones that start with an underscore.
